questions.question: What are the essential Docker commands every developer should know?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can perform basic Docker operations independently without needing constant help from senior developers during daily development work
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing commands without understanding the image versus container lifecycle — freshers often try to remove images with docker rm instead of docker rmi or wonder why docker stop doesn't delete the container
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention docker exec -it container_name /bin/bash for debugging running containers and docker system df to check disk usage — shows you've gone beyond tutorials and debugged real issues

questions.direct_answer: Essential Docker commands include docker build to create images from Dockerfiles, docker run to start containers, docker ps to list running containers, docker stop and docker rm to halt and remove containers, docker images to view local images, docker logs to read container output, and docker pull to download images from registries like Docker Hub.

rows: Build image from Dockerfile in current dir

answer_sections.content: The commands I use most day-to-day are: docker build -t myapp:1.0 . to build the image, docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0 to start it, docker ps to see what's running, and docker logs containerId to see what the app is printing. If I need to debug inside a container, docker exec -it containerId bash opens an interactive shell. docker stop and docker rm to clean up. The -d flag for detached mode runs the container in background — useful so the terminal isn't taken over by container logs. For working with compose, docker-compose up and docker-compose down replace most individual container management.

items: docker build -t myapp:1.0 . — build an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory
docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0 — start a container and map the port
docker run -d myapp:1.0 — start in detached (background) mode so your terminal stays free
docker ps — see what containers are currently running
docker logs -f containerId — follow the app's log output in real time
docker exec -it containerId bash — open a shell inside the running container
docker stop / docker rm — stop and clean up a container
docker images — list all locally available images

beats.text: On a real team the most-used trio is docker run, docker ps, and docker logs. If the app isn't starting, docker logs shows the Spring Boot stack trace exactly as if you ran it locally.

sections.title: Docker Command Essentials for Daily Development
sections.content:
Docker commands fall into three categories: **image management** (building and storing templates), **container lifecycle** (running and stopping instances), and **inspection** (viewing what's happening). Think of images as compiled JAR files and containers as running JVM processes — you build the image once, then run multiple containers from it.

The confusion happens because Docker uses similar names: **docker run** starts containers, **docker images** lists templates, **docker ps** shows active processes. Understanding this split prevents the classic mistake of trying to start an image or delete a running container without stopping it first. Most day-to-day work uses seven commands: build to create, run to start, ps to check status, logs to debug, stop to halt, rm to clean up containers, and rmi to delete images. The **docker exec** command enters running containers for live debugging — essential when your Spring Boot app starts but behaves incorrectly.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Build and Run|~Create and start|docker build -t app .|docker run -p 8080:8080|-d for background
blue|Inspect|~See what's happening|docker ps (-a for all)|docker logs -f|docker exec -it bash
emerald|Cleanup|~Free space|docker stop and rm|docker rmi for images|docker system prune
violet|Mental Model|~Image vs container|image is the JAR file|container is the running JVM|rm vs rmi differ

sections.title: Common Docker Command Workflow
When You Need Each Command
sections.content:
Use **docker build** whenever you change application code or dependencies — every time you modify your Spring Boot app.

Use **docker run** to start fresh containers for testing or when configuration changes require a clean state.

Use **docker ps** constantly during development to verify containers started correctly and see their status.

Use **docker logs** immediately when something breaks — it's your first debugging step before diving deeper.

Use **docker exec** when logs aren't enough and you need to check filesystem contents, test network connectivity with curl, or run SQL queries against an embedded database.

Use **docker stop** and **docker rm** when you need to free ports or want to start with a clean configuration after testing.

Use **docker system prune** weekly to reclaim disk space consumed by old images and stopped containers.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing images and containers**: Freshers try docker rm on an image or docker rmi on a running container, getting cryptic errors. Remember images are templates, containers are instances — you can't remove a template while instances are using it.
- **Forgetting the -d flag in docker run**: Without detached mode, your terminal hangs and you can't run other commands. You end up with multiple terminal windows instead of running containers in the background.
- **Using docker ps without -a**: You only see running containers, so when your container crashes immediately after starting, docker ps shows nothing and you think Docker is broken. Always use docker ps -a to see stopped containers and their exit codes.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **docker build**: creates immutable images from Dockerfiles — run this after every code change
**docker run**: starts new containers from images — use -d for background, -p for port mapping, --name for easy reference
**docker ps**: lists containers — add -a to see stopped ones, essential for debugging startup failures
**docker logs**: shows container stdout/stderr — use -f to follow in real time like tail -f
**docker exec**: runs commands inside running containers — docker exec -it container_name /bin/bash opens interactive shell
**docker stop/rm**: lifecycle management — stop halts gracefully, rm deletes the container entirely
**docker system prune**: bulk cleanup — removes stopped containers, unused images, dangling build cache in one command

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd say the essential Docker commands break into three groups. First, for building and running, you've got docker build to create images from your Dockerfile and docker run to start containers from those images. When I'm developing a Spring Boot app, I use docker build after every code change and docker run with the -d flag to start it in the background. Second, for monitoring what's happening, there's docker ps to list running containers and docker logs to see application output. I always use docker logs -f to follow logs in real time when I'm testing new features. The -f flag is crucial because otherwise you're constantly rerunning the command. Third, for debugging and cleanup, docker exec lets you open a shell inside a running container — that's super helpful when logs aren't enough and you need to check if a file exists or test network connectivity. Then docker stop and docker rm handle shutdown and removal. One mistake I see a lot is people forgetting that images and containers are different — you can't docker rm an image, you need docker rmi for that. Also, it's worth knowing docker system prune to clean up disk space, because Docker caches everything and you can easily end up with 20 gigs of old images after a few weeks. The key is understanding the image-container relationship — images are like JAR files, containers are like running JVM processes.

questions.question: What does docker run -p 8080:8080 mean?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Docker's network isolation — containers run in separate network namespaces and require explicit port mapping to be accessible from the host machine
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking containers automatically expose ports — freshers forget the -p flag, then can't figure out why curl localhost:8080 returns connection refused even though the container is running
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that you can map different ports like -p 9090:8080 to avoid conflicts when port 8080 is already in use by another service, and mention that you can bind to specific interfaces with -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080

questions.direct_answer: The -p flag maps ports between your host machine and the container. The format is -p host_port:container_port, so -p 8080:8080 means traffic to localhost:8080 on your machine gets forwarded to port 8080 inside the container where your Spring Boot application listens. Without this mapping, the container's network is isolated and unreachable from your host.

answer_sections.content:
# host_port:container_port
docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp  # standard mapping
docker run -p 9090:8080 myapp  # host 9090 → container 8080
docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 8443:8443 myapp  # multiple ports

# Container runs on port 8080 internally (EXPOSE 8080)
# -p makes it accessible from outside the container

The -p flag maps a port on your host machine to a port inside the container. The format is host:container. So -p 8080:8080 means when you browse to localhost:8080, Docker forwards that request to port 8080 inside the container where Spring Boot is listening. The EXPOSE instruction in Dockerfile only documents which port the app uses — it doesn't actually publish it. The -p flag is what actually makes the port accessible from outside the container. If you run docker run without -p, the container runs but you can't access it from your browser.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app running in a container, accessed from the browser
speakable_v2.hook: Without the -p flag, your Spring Boot container runs perfectly — and you still can't reach it from your browser. Port mapping is the missing piece.

beats.text: The -p flag maps a port on your host machine to a port inside the container. Format is host_port:container_port. So -p 8080:8080 means requests to localhost:8080 on your machine are forwarded to port 8080 inside the container.
If you want Spring Boot running on container port 8080 but accessible on host port 9090, use -p 9090:8080. Your browser hits localhost:9090, Docker forwards it to container port 8080.

Containers are isolated by default. Their ports are not visible outside the container network. -p explicitly punches a hole from the host into the container. You can map multiple ports with multiple -p flags.

candidates miss: EXPOSE 8080 in the Dockerfile is just documentation — it does not publish the port. Only docker run -p actually makes the port reachable. This is one of the most common Docker gotchas for beginners.

speakable_v2.cap: Remember the format as 'outside:inside' — left side is what you type in your browser, right side is where the container is actually listening.

sections.title: Understanding Docker Port Mapping
sections.content:
Docker containers run in **isolated network namespaces** — think of each container as having its own private localhost. When your Spring Boot app starts inside a container and listens on port 8080, that's port 8080 in the container's private network, not your machine's network. The **-p flag** creates a tunnel from a port on your host to a port in the container. The syntax **-p host_port:container_port** maps them: traffic arriving at the host port gets forwarded into the container port. So **-p 8080:8080** means requests to localhost:8080 on your development machine reach port 8080 inside the container.

Without this mapping, the container is like a server in a locked room — it's running, but you can't reach it. The confusion happens because in non-containerized development, your Spring Boot app just binds to 8080 and you immediately access it. With Docker, you need to explicitly punch a hole through the container's network boundary. You can map any host port to any container port: **-p 9090:8080** avoids conflicts if another service already uses 8080 on your machine.

sections.content:
amber|Port Mapping|~host colon container|-p 8080:8080|left is your machine|right is inside container
blue|Why Needed|~Containers are isolated|private network|-p punches a hole|EXPOSE is only docs
emerald|Patterns|~Flexible mapping|-p 9090:8080 avoids conflict|multiple -p flags|127.0.0.1 binds local
violet|Common Trap|~Forgot the -p|container runs fine|localhost refuses|nothing reachable

sections.title: Port Mapping Scenarios
When to Use Different Port Mapping Patterns
sections.content:
Use **-p 8080:8080** for standard development when you want the container port to match your usual local port — makes it easy to remember and switch between containerized and non-containerized setups.

Use **-p 9090:8080** when port 8080 is already occupied by another service or container — this happens constantly in microservices development when running multiple services simultaneously.

Use **multiple -p flags** like -p 8080:8080 -p 5005:5005 when your container exposes multiple ports — HTTP on 8080 plus a remote debugger on 5005 or a metrics endpoint on 9091.

Use **-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080** when the service should only be accessible from your local machine, not from the network — adds security for databases or admin interfaces.

Use **-p without host port** like -p 8080 to let Docker assign a random available port — useful in automated testing where you don't care about the specific port number.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting the -p flag entirely**: Freshers run docker run without port mapping, see the container running with docker ps, then spend an hour debugging why localhost:8080 doesn't work. The container is fine — it's listening on 8080 inside its network — but that network is isolated from your host.
- **Reversing the port order**: Using -p 8080:9090 when you meant -p 9090:8080 leads to confusing errors. The pattern is always host first, container second. Remember the traffic flows from left to right: from your machine into the container.
- **Not checking for port conflicts**: Running docker run -p 8080:8080 when another container or local process already uses 8080 fails with a bind error. Use docker ps to see what's using ports, or use a different host port like 9090.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **-p host_port:container_port**: maps ports from your machine to the container — traffic flows left to right
**Network isolation**: containers have private localhost — without -p, services inside are unreachable from host
**Same or different ports**: -p 8080:8080 keeps consistency, -p 9090:8080 avoids conflicts with other services
**Multiple mappings**: use multiple -p flags to expose several ports from one container — HTTP, debugger, metrics
**Interface binding**: -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 restricts access to localhost only — more secure for sensitive services
**Random port assignment**: -p 8080 without host port lets Docker choose — useful in CI/CD pipelines
**EXPOSE in Dockerfile**: documents which ports the container uses but doesn't publish them — -p is still required

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The -p flag maps ports between your host machine and the container. The format is -p followed by host port, colon, container port. So -p 8080:8080 means when you hit localhost:8080 on your machine, Docker forwards that traffic to port 8080 inside the container. The reason you need this is that containers run in isolated networks — each container has its own private localhost. When your Spring Boot app starts in a container and listens on 8080, that's port 8080 in the container's network, not your machine's network. Without the -p flag, you can't reach it even though the container is running. A common pattern I use is -p 9090:8080 when I'm running multiple services and port 8080 is already taken by something else. The container still listens on 8080 internally, but I access it through 9090 on my host. That's really useful in microservices development. You can also map multiple ports with multiple -p flags, like -p 8080:8080 -p 5005:5005 if you want to attach a debugger to your containerized app. One mistake I see freshers make is forgetting the -p flag completely, then wondering why localhost:8080 doesn't work. The container is actually fine and listening, but it's in a separate network namespace. Another mistake is reversing the order — the host port always comes first, then the container port. It helps to think of it as traffic flowing from left to right, from your machine into the container.

questions.question: How do you view logs from a running Docker container?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can independently debug containerized applications by reading application output — a fundamental skill since containers hide the usual console output you see in local development
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the -f flag for real-time logs — freshers repeatedly run docker logs instead of following the stream, missing events between executions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention combining --since with --tail for targeted debugging like docker logs --since 5m --tail 50 to see recent errors without scrolling through gigabytes of historical logs

questions.direct_answer: Use docker logs followed by the container ID or name to see all output from a container. For example, docker logs order-api shows stdout and stderr. Add -f to follow logs in real time like tail -f, --tail 100 to see only the last 100 lines, and --since 10m to view logs from the last 10 minutes. Combine flags for targeted debugging.

answer_sections.content:
# See all logs
docker logs my-app-container

# Follow live (like tail -f)
docker logs -f my-app-container

# Last 100 lines
docker logs --tail 100 my-app-container

# Logs since 30 minutes ago
docker logs --since 30m my-app-container

# Get container ID first
docker ps  # shows container IDs

docker logs is essential for debugging. By default it shows all logs since the container started. I almost always use docker logs -f to follow the logs in real time — it stays open and shows new log lines as they appear, like tail -f on a log file. For a container that's producing a lot of logs, --tail 100 limits output to the last 100 lines so you don't get overwhelmed. If your Spring Boot app isn't starting correctly, docker logs will show the stack trace and tell you exactly what went wrong — same logs as if you ran it locally.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app failing to start inside a Docker container
speakable_v2.hook: When your containerized Spring Boot app silently fails, docker logs is the first place you look — and docker logs -f is the command you'll use every day.

beats.text: docker logs shows everything the application wrote to stdout and stderr since the container started. For a Spring Boot app, that's all the application log output — including stack traces, startup messages, and errors.

items: docker logs containerId — dump all logs since container started
docker logs -f containerId — follow live, like tail -f on a log file
docker logs --tail 100 containerId — only the last 100 lines
docker logs --since 30m containerId — logs from the last 30 minutes

beats.text: If a Spring Boot container crashes on startup, docker logs shows the full stack trace — same output as running the app locally. No guessing required.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: if Spring Boot is writing logs to a file inside the container instead of stdout, docker logs will show nothing. Configure logging to stdout in container environments — that's where Docker expects to collect logs.

sections.title: Reading Container Logs for Debugging
sections.content:
When you run a Spring Boot app locally, you see console output immediately in your terminal. With Docker, that output goes into the container's isolated environment.

The **docker logs** command retrieves stdout and stderr from a container and displays them on your host machine. You reference the container by name or ID: **docker logs order-api** or **docker logs a3f8b2c1**. By default, this dumps the entire log history and exits — fine for quick checks but impractical for debugging active issues. The **-f flag** (follow) works like tail -f, streaming new log lines as they appear. This is essential when testing API endpoints or watching for errors in real time. The **--tail N flag** shows only the last N lines, preventing your terminal from being flooded with thousands of startup messages. The **--since flag** filters by time: --since 10m shows logs from the last 10 minutes, --since 2023-12-01 shows everything after a specific date. Combining these flags creates powerful debugging workflows: **docker logs --since 5m --tail 100 -f order-api** follows recent logs without historical noise.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Basics|~Read app output|docker logs name|stdout and stderr|same as local console
blue|Live Follow|~The -f flag|streams new lines|like tail -f|daily debugging
emerald|Trim Output|~Focus on recent|--tail 100|--since 10m|combine flags
violet|Gotcha|~Logs must hit stdout|file appender means blank|configure stdout|crashed means no new lines

sections.title: Common Log Viewing Patterns
When to Use Each Log Command Pattern
sections.content:
Use **docker logs container_name** without flags for quick health checks — did the app start successfully, are there any obvious errors in recent output.

Use **docker logs -f** during active development when testing new features or API endpoints — you need to see responses and errors as they happen, just like watching console output in local development.

Use **docker logs --tail 50** when you suspect a recent error but don't want to scroll through hundreds of startup log lines — Spring Boot initialization is verbose and you care about what happened in the last few seconds.

Use **docker logs --since 10m** when investigating an issue reported at a specific time — a user complained 5 minutes ago, so you check logs from that timeframe.

Use **docker logs --since 5m --tail 100 -f** as your standard debugging command — start with recent logs, then follow new ones, avoiding historical noise.

Use **docker logs container_name | grep ERROR** to scan for exceptions across all output when you don't know when the problem occurred.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not using -f for real-time debugging**: Freshers run docker logs repeatedly in a loop, hitting up-arrow and Enter, missing events between executions. Using -f keeps the stream open so you see every log line as it happens — critical when testing API calls or watching for specific errors.
- **Overwhelming the terminal with historical logs**: Running docker logs without --tail on a container that's been running for hours dumps thousands of lines, making it impossible to find recent errors. Always use --tail or --since to limit output.
- **Forgetting containers stop writing logs after exit**: If the container crashed, docker logs shows output up to the crash, but no new lines appear even with -f. Check docker ps -a to see if the container exited, then read logs to find the cause.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **docker logs container_name**: shows all stdout and stderr from the container — your primary debugging tool
**-f flag**: follows logs in real time like tail -f — essential during active development and testing
**--tail N**: limits output to last N lines — prevents terminal flooding from verbose Spring Boot startup logs
**--since**: filters by time — --since 10m shows last 10 minutes, --since 2h shows last 2 hours
**Combining flags**: docker logs --since 5m --tail 100 -f gives targeted real-time debugging without historical noise
**-t flag**: adds timestamps to each line — useful when correlating logs with external events or user reports
**Piping to grep**: docker logs container_name | grep ERROR scans for exceptions across all output

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To view logs from a running Docker container, you use the docker logs command followed by the container name or ID. So if my container is called order-api, I'd run docker logs order-api. That shows all the output — everything your Spring Boot app wrote to stdout and stderr. But in practice, I almost always use the -f flag to follow logs in real time, like docker logs -f order-api. That's crucial during development because you want to see what happens when you call an API endpoint or trigger some feature. Without -f, you're constantly rerunning the command and missing events between executions. Now, if the container has been running for a while, docker logs dumps thousands of lines and you can't find anything useful. That's where --tail comes in. I use docker logs --tail 50 order-api to see just the last 50 lines, which skips all the Spring Boot startup noise and shows recent activity. Another really helpful flag is --since for filtering by time. Like docker logs --since 10m shows logs from the last 10 minutes. I combine these when debugging: docker logs --since 5m --tail 100 -f order-api. That starts with the last 100 lines from the last 5 minutes, then follows new output. It's perfect for investigating an error that just happened without scrolling through historical logs. One thing freshers forget is that once a container stops, logs stop too. If you're using -f and nothing appears, check docker ps -a to see if the container crashed. Then run docker logs without -f to see what happened before it died.

questions.question: How do you clean up Docker resources (stopped containers, unused images)?

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness that Docker consumes significant disk space through layer caching and stopped containers — a practical operational skill that prevents your development machine from running out of disk after weeks of use
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Docker caches everything aggressively — freshers are surprised when Docker uses 20GB of disk after a few weeks of development and don't know how to reclaim it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention docker system df to check disk usage before cleanup and explain the difference between dangling images and unused images — shows systematic approach rather than blindly deleting everything

questions.direct_answer: Use docker system prune to remove all stopped containers, unused images, and dangling build cache in one command. For targeted cleanup, docker container prune removes only stopped containers and docker image prune removes unused images. To delete specific items, use docker rm for containers and docker rmi for images. Check disk usage first with docker system df.

answer_sections.content:
# Remove all stopped containers
docker container prune

# Remove unused images
docker image prune

# Remove EVERYTHING unused (nuclear option)
docker system prune
docker system prune -a  # also removes unused images

# Check disk usage
docker system df

Docker can eat up a lot of disk space if you don't clean up. Stopped containers, old images, and build cache accumulate. docker system prune removes stopped containers and dangling images in one shot. docker system prune -a is more aggressive and removes all images not currently used by a running container — useful on a laptop that's getting full. I run docker system df to see how much space Docker is using before deciding what to clean. On CI servers, cleanup scripts run automatically. On local machines, occasional docker system prune keeps things tidy.

follow_up_questions: What is a dangling image in Docker?
How do you automatically remove a container when it stops?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Developer laptop running low on disk space from accumulated Docker images
speakable_v2.hook: Docker is quietly accumulating stopped containers and old images on your machine — and you won't notice until your laptop's disk is full.

beats.text: Every docker build creates new image layers. Every docker run creates a stopped container when it finishes. Neither is cleaned up automatically. Over weeks of development, this adds up fast.

items: docker system df — check how much disk space Docker is using
docker container prune — remove all stopped containers
docker image prune — remove dangling images (untagged)
docker system prune — remove stopped containers, dangling images, and unused build cache
docker system prune -a — also removes images not used by any running container

beats.text: A dangling image is one that's been replaced by a newer build but still takes up space — its tag was reassigned to the new image and it now shows as none:none in docker images. docker image prune removes these.

production trap: docker system prune -a on a production machine removes all images not currently running — including images for services that are temporarily stopped. Use with care outside of local dev.

speakable_v2.cap: Run docker system prune periodically on your dev machine. On CI, cleanup jobs usually run automatically. Knowing the difference between prune and prune -a stops you from accidentally deleting needed images.

sections.title: Managing Docker Disk Usage
sections.content:
Docker consumes disk space aggressively through **layer caching**. Every time you run docker build, Docker saves intermediate layers so future builds reuse them — this speeds up builds dramatically but accumulates gigabytes of data. **Stopped containers** persist on disk even after you stop them, storing their entire filesystem state in case you want to restart or inspect them. **Dangling images** are layers that aren't tagged and aren't referenced by any container — they're leftovers from rebuilds when you reuse the same tag. After a few weeks of development, you can easily hit 20-30 GB of Docker data without realizing it. The **docker system prune** command is the nuclear option: it removes all stopped containers, all networks not used by at least one container, all dangling images, and all dangling build cache. For surgical cleanup, **docker container prune** removes only stopped containers, and **docker image prune** removes only unused images. Use **docker system df** to see how much space Docker consumes before deciding what to clean.

The key is understanding that Docker prioritizes performance through caching — it never automatically deletes anything.

blue|Check First|~Measure usage|docker system df|images, containers, cache|decide what to cut
emerald|Targeted|~Surgical cleanup|container prune|image prune|rm and rmi specifics
violet|Nuclear|~Broad sweep|system prune|-a removes unused images|careful in prod

sections.title: Docker Cleanup Commands
When to Use Each Cleanup Command
sections.content:
Use **docker system df** weekly or when disk space warnings appear — it shows how much space Docker consumes across images, containers, volumes, and build cache, helping you decide what to clean.

Use **docker system prune** as routine maintenance every few weeks during active development — it reclaims space from stopped test containers and dangling layers without affecting your current work.

Use **docker system prune -a** when disk space is critically low or before major version upgrades — this removes all unused images, not just dangling ones, so you'll need to rebuild or re-pull images on next use.

Use **docker container prune** when you've been running lots of temporary test containers and want to keep your image cache intact.

Use **docker image prune** when you've rebuilt the same image many times and know old versions are safe to delete.

Use **docker rm** and **docker rmi** for targeted deletion of specific containers or images during debugging when you want precise control.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing Docker caches everything**: Freshers run docker build dozens of times during a feature, never realizing that each failed build leaves layers behind. Weeks later, Docker uses 25GB and they think it's a bug. Running docker system df reveals the truth — build cache alone can hit 15GB.
- **Confusing docker rm and docker rmi**: Trying to delete an image with docker rm order-service:v1 fails with a confusing error. Remember: rm for containers (running instances), rmi for images (templates). The names are frustratingly similar.
- **Pruning without checking first**: Running docker system prune -a blindly deletes all unused images, forcing you to rebuild or re-download everything on next use. Always run docker system df first to see what you're about to delete and whether it's worth the rebuild cost.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **docker system df**: shows disk usage breakdown — images, containers, volumes, build cache — run this before cleanup
**docker system prune**: removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, build cache — safe routine maintenance
**docker system prune -a**: more aggressive — includes all unused images, not just dangling ones, may require rebuilds
**docker container prune**: removes only stopped containers — useful when you want to keep image cache intact
**docker image prune**: removes only dangling images — layers no longer referenced by any tagged image
**docker rm vs docker rmi**: rm deletes containers, rmi deletes images — mixing these up causes confusing errors
**Layer caching**: Docker saves every intermediate build step — fast builds but consumes gigabytes over time

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Docker cleanup is something every developer needs to know because Docker consumes disk space really aggressively through layer caching. Every time you build an image, Docker saves intermediate layers so future builds are faster. That's great for performance, but after a few weeks of development, you can easily have 20 or 30 gigs of Docker data. The first thing I do is run docker system df to see how much space Docker is using. That breaks down disk usage into images, containers, volumes, and build cache. Once I know what's consuming space, I use docker system prune to clean up. That removes all stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, and build cache in one command. It's safe for routine maintenance because it only deletes things you're not actively using. If I need more aggressive cleanup, there's docker system prune -a, which also removes unused images, not just dangling ones. The trade-off is you'll need to rebuild or re-pull those images on next use, so I only do that when disk space is critically low. For targeted cleanup, docker container prune removes just stopped containers, and docker image prune removes just unused images. If I want precise control, I use docker rm for specific containers and docker rmi for specific images. One mistake I see freshers make is not realizing Docker caches everything. They build an image 50 times while debugging, never cleaning up, then wonder why Docker uses 20 gigs. Another mistake is confusing docker rm and docker rmi — rm is for containers, rmi is for images. The key is to make cleanup part of your routine, maybe run docker system prune every couple weeks, so disk usage doesn't sneak up on you.

questions.question: How do you debug a running Docker container — what commands do you use?
questions.title: Debugging a Running Docker Container
questions.direct_answer: Use docker logs to see application output and errors, docker exec -it container_name /bin/bash to open an interactive shell inside the running container for filesystem inspection and command execution, and docker inspect container_name to view detailed configuration including environment variables, network settings, port mappings, and volume mounts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Operational debugging ability — whether you can diagnose issues in containerized environments without constant help from senior developers, a critical skill for modern Java backend work
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing docker logs — freshers can read output but can't investigate deeper issues like missing files, network connectivity, or environment configuration
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention docker stats for real-time CPU and memory usage monitoring and docker top to see running processes — shows awareness of performance debugging beyond just application logs

sections.title: Debugging Running Containers
sections.content:
Debugging containerized applications requires different tools than local development. You can't just open a file explorer or attach a debugger with one click — containers are isolated environments.

The **docker logs** command is your first stop: it shows stdout and stderr, revealing startup errors, exceptions, and application output. But logs only tell part of the story. Sometimes you need to see if a configuration file exists, check network connectivity, or verify environment variables. That's where **docker exec** comes in. Running **docker exec -it container_name /bin/bash** opens an interactive shell inside the running container, giving you full access to the filesystem and tools like curl, ls, cat, and env. You're literally inside the container's namespace, seeing exactly what the application sees. For configuration inspection, **docker inspect** dumps a massive JSON object containing everything about the container: environment variables, port mappings, volume mounts, network settings, and resource limits. This is crucial when your app behaves differently in Docker versus locally — often the issue is a missing environment variable or incorrect volume mount. Advanced debugging includes **docker stats** for real-time CPU and memory usage, and **docker top** to see running processes inside the container.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|docker logs|~First stop|-f to follow|--tail to trim|shows stack traces
blue|docker exec -it|~Get inside|open a /bin/bash shell|check files, env, curl|-i stdin, -t tty
emerald|docker inspect|~Config as JSON|env vars and ports|volumes and network|local vs Docker diffs
violet|Performance|~Resource view|docker stats|live CPU and memory|docker top processes

sections.title: Container Debugging Workflow
When to Use Each Debugging Command
sections.content:
Use **docker logs -f** as your first debugging step for any issue — if the app throws exceptions or fails to start, logs reveal the problem 80% of the time.

Use **docker exec -it container_name /bin/bash** when logs aren't enough and you need to verify filesystem state — check if a configuration file got copied into the image, see if the application JAR exists in the right location, or test network connectivity with curl to other services.

Use **docker inspect** when behavior differs between local and Docker environments — the issue is often a missing environment variable, incorrect port mapping, or volume mount pointing to the wrong path.

Use **docker stats** when the app runs but performs poorly — shows real-time CPU and memory usage, revealing if you're hitting container resource limits or if the JVM is consuming unexpected memory.

Use **docker top** to see what processes are actually running inside the container — useful when a shell script launches multiple processes and you need to verify they're all alive.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only using docker logs**: Freshers stop at logs and give up when the error isn't obvious. They don't realize they can open a shell with docker exec and poke around inside the container to check files, test commands, or verify configuration.
- **Forgetting -it flags on docker exec**: Running docker exec without -i -t results in non-interactive or missing terminal output. The -it combination is essential — -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a pseudo-TTY for proper terminal behavior.
- **Not having debugging tools in the image**: Opening a shell with docker exec only to find curl, wget, and even ls are missing because the base image is Alpine or a distroless variant. Production images strip unnecessary tools, but during debugging you need them — either use a different base image for dev or install tools temporarily.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **docker logs**: first debugging step — shows stdout/stderr, use -f to follow in real time, --tail to limit output
**docker exec -it container_name /bin/bash**: opens interactive shell inside running container — full access to filesystem and commands
**docker inspect**: dumps complete container configuration as JSON — environment variables, ports, volumes, network settings
**docker stats**: real-time CPU and memory usage — essential for performance debugging and resource limit issues
**docker top**: shows running processes inside container — verify services started correctly in multi-process containers
**-it flags**: required for interactive shell — -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates pseudo-TTY for terminal behavior
**Base image tools**: Alpine and distroless images lack debugging utilities — use fuller base images in development

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When I need to debug a running Docker container, I use three main commands. First is docker logs, usually with the -f flag to follow in real time. That's my starting point because most issues show up in application output — startup errors, exceptions, failed database connections. I run docker logs --tail 100 -f container_name to see recent logs and keep watching. If logs don't reveal the problem, I use docker exec to open a shell inside the container. The command is docker exec -it container_name /bin/bash. That drops me into an interactive bash session where I can poke around. I can check if configuration files exist with ls, verify environment variables with env, or test network connectivity with curl. It's like SSH-ing into a server — you have full access to the filesystem and can run commands to investigate. The -it flags are important — -i keeps stdin open and -t gives you a proper terminal. Third is docker inspect for configuration issues. That dumps a huge JSON object with everything about the container — environment variables, port mappings, volume mounts, network settings. I use it when the app behaves differently in Docker versus locally, because usually it's a missing environment variable or wrong volume mount. Beyond those three, docker stats is helpful for performance issues. It shows real-time CPU and memory usage, so you can see if you're hitting resource limits. And docker top shows running processes inside the container, which is useful if you have multiple services in one container and need to verify they all started. One mistake freshers make is stopping at docker logs and not knowing they can open a shell. Another is forgetting the -it flags on docker exec, which results in a weird non-interactive session. The key is to think of containers as isolated environments you can inspect from the outside with logs and inspect, or step inside with exec to investigate directly.
